_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss in another section (Selin's beginners' workshops vs Morag's apprentice; Gareth's gas bill vs Morag's prices). Used by the Part 7 practice page.
title: Made by hand
subtitle: Four craftspeople describe the traditional skills they practise.

sections.A: Selin, 38, paper marbler. Marbling means floating drops of paint on a tray of thickened water, combing them into patterns, and then laying a sheet of paper on top to lift the design off. It sounds simple. In my first year, every single sheet I made went in the bin: the colours sank, ran together or just turned into brown mud. My teacher, an elderly man in a workshop near the harbour, simply kept saying 'Again.' Eventually something clicked. What I love most is that no two sheets can ever be the same, however hard I try; the paint moves in its own way every time, so each one is completely unique. Most of my paper goes to bookbinders and stationery makers. I also run weekend workshops for beginners, and I warn them on day one that their first efforts will look like soup.
sections.B: Gareth, 46, glass-blower. I first saw glass being blown when I was eight, on a family holiday, and I stood watching the man at the furnace for so long that my parents had to drag me away. Thirty-eight years later, it's what I do every day. The furnace runs at over eleven hundred degrees, and you're constantly turning the pipe, blowing and shaping before the glass cools. I work with an assistant, Ellie, and after six years together we hardly speak while we're making something. She knows when I need the next tool before I've reached for it. It's hot, tiring and occasionally painful work; I've stopped counting the burns. The thing that keeps me awake at night isn't the danger, though. It's the gas bill. A furnace has to stay lit around the clock, and that costs a fortune.
sections.C: Morag, 61, basket-weaver. I grow my own willow on a strip of land beside the house, about twenty different varieties, each with its own colour, from deep purple to bright orange. I cut it in winter, dry it, then soak it before weaving so that it bends instead of snapping. A good log basket takes me most of a day. The difficulty is that people see a basket and expect to pay what they'd pay in a supermarket, and they're quite shocked when I explain the price reflects a full day's labour, never mind the year it took to grow the willow. Not many young people take up the craft now, which worries me. That's why, for the last eighteen months, I've had an apprentice, a nineteen-year-old called Duncan. He's patient, he's careful, and his baskets are already better than mine were at his age.
sections.D: Jun, 29, bookbinder. I trained at a college in London, but most of what I know I learned afterwards, working for an old binder called Mr Ashworth. When he retired, he gave me his entire workshop: presses, knives and brass tools, some more than a hundred years old. I still use them every day, and they work better than anything new. Much of my work is repairing books rather than making new ones. Libraries send me rare volumes, but the jobs I remember are the family ones: a grandmother's cookbook held together with tape, a Bible with generations of birthdays written inside. These books are rarely worth much money, but to their owners they're priceless. Last month a man collected his late father's poetry notebook and stood in my workshop crying. Moments like that are why I'd never do anything else.

questions.question: Which person failed completely when they first tried the craft?
questions.why: 'In my first year, every single sheet I made went in the bin.'

questions.question: Which person produces their own raw material?
questions.why: 'I grow my own willow on a strip of land beside the house.'

questions.question: Which person works so closely with a colleague that words are hardly needed?
questions.why: 'We hardly speak… She knows when I need the next tool before I've reached for it.'

questions.question: Which person says the objects they work on are often valued for emotional reasons?
questions.why: 'These books are rarely worth much money, but to their owners they're priceless.'

questions.question: Which person can never repeat a piece exactly?
questions.why: 'No two sheets can ever be the same, however hard I try.'

questions.question: Which person is worried about the expense of keeping equipment running?
questions.why: 'It's the gas bill. A furnace has to stay lit around the clock.' Morag worries about prices, but that is about what customers will pay.

questions.question: Which person is training a young person to continue the craft?
questions.why: 'I've had an apprentice, a nineteen-year-old called Duncan.' Selin teaches beginners at weekend workshops, not one person over time.

questions.question: Which person uses tools that were handed on by someone else?
questions.why: Mr Ashworth 'gave me his entire workshop… I still use them every day'.

questions.question: Which person became fascinated by the craft as a child?
questions.why: At eight, 'I stood watching the man at the furnace for so long that my parents had to drag me away.' Selin had a teacher, but she does not mention her childhood.

questions.question: Which person feels customers do not understand why their work costs what it does?
questions.why: People 'expect to pay what they'd pay in a supermarket… quite shocked when I explain the price'.
